title: Working With Travel Creators and Influencers for Your Stay
excerpt: How hotels and homestays can choose travel creators by audience fit, decide between barter and paid stays, write a simple brief, handle disclosure and content rights, and measure bookings.
description: How hotels and homestays can work with travel creators: audience fit, barter vs paid stays, briefs, disclosure rules in India and tracking bookings.
html:
To work well with travel creators, choose them by how closely their audience matches your guests, not by follower count. Decide whether a free stay or a paid fee fits the work, agree a short written brief covering deliverables, dates and content rights, make sure posts carry clear ad disclosure, and track enquiries and bookings with a unique link or code.

Decide what you want from a creator

Creators can do three different jobs for a hotel or homestay, and it helps to know which one you are paying for:

  • Reach: introducing your property to people who have not heard of it.
  • Proof: showing what the stay is really like, in a voice guests trust more than your own.
  • Content: photos and video you can use on your own website, OTA listings and Instagram.

A small property often gets most value from the second and third. Reach is useful, but only if the people reached can actually come to you.

Choose creators by audience fit, not follower count

A creator with a large following of international backpackers is unlikely to fill a family farmstay near Mysuru. A creator with a modest following of Bengaluru families who take weekend drives might. Look at who follows and engages, not just how many.

What to check before you reach out

CheckHow to judge it
Audience locationAsk for a screenshot of their audience insights showing top cities and countries
Audience typeRead comments: are they couples, families, solo travellers, bikers, workation seekers?
Content styleDoes their work suit your property: slow and calm, adventurous, luxury, budget?
Engagement qualityReal questions in comments ("where is this?", "how much per night?") rather than only emojis
Past stay contentHow they covered other properties; whether disclosure was clear
HonestyDo they ever mention downsides? Guests trust creators who do

Your own past guests who create content are often the best fit of all. They already know the property and their audience resembles your guests.

Barter stays versus paid collaborations

Most small properties start with barter: a complimentary stay in exchange for content. That can work, but be clear about what is being exchanged.

  • Barter suits smaller creators, off-season dates and simple deliverables such as a few stories and one post. Work out its real cost: room nights you could otherwise sell, meals, activities and staff time.
  • Paid collaborations suit creators whose content you plan to reuse widely, or who need to travel far, or where you want specific deliverables like a short video for your website.
  • Hybrid arrangements (a stay plus a modest fee) are common for mid-sized creators.

As an example only: if a two-night stay for two with meals would sell for ₹16,000 in peak season, that is the true cost of a barter collaboration on those dates. Offering the same stay midweek in the off-season costs you far less in lost revenue.

Write a simple brief and agreement

A one or two page document avoids most disagreements. It does not need to be complicated, but it should be in writing, even if that is a clear email or WhatsApp message both sides confirm.

What the brief should cover

  1. Dates and what is included: number of nights, guests, meals, activities, transport if any.
  2. Deliverables: for example, one reel, one carousel post and a set of stories, with rough posting dates.
  3. Key facts to mention: location, how to reach, what makes the stay different, how to book (your website or WhatsApp).
  4. What not to say: anything inaccurate, such as "beachfront" if you are a short walk away, or claims you cannot support.
  5. Disclosure: that the content must be clearly labelled as a collaboration or advertisement.
  6. Content rights: whether you can reuse their photos and video, where, and for how long.
  7. Tags and links: your handle, location tag and a tracking link or code.
  8. Fee and payment terms, if any.

Give the creator freedom on style. The brief sets facts and boundaries, not a script.

Disclosure rules in India

Paid or gifted collaborations must be disclosed. Two sets of guidance are relevant:

  • The Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) issued its Guidelines for Influencer Advertising in Digital Media in May 2021. They list labels such as "Advertisement", "Ad", "Sponsored", "Collaboration", "Partnership" and "Free gift", and say the label must be easy to notice, not hidden in a bio, at the end of a post, among hashtags or behind "more". For pictures or videos without text, the label should appear on the image or video itself. ASCI treats free products, trips and media barters as material connections that need disclosure.
  • The Department of Consumer Affairs released "Endorsement Know-hows!" in January 2023 for celebrities and influencers, under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. It asks endorsers to disclose any material connection, including free or discounted products and trips, prominently and in clear terms such as "advertisement", "sponsored" or "paid promotion", and not to endorse what they have not personally used or experienced. The Department of Consumer Affairs release summarises it.

In practice: write the disclosure requirement into your brief, check the posts when they go live, and ask for a correction if the label is missing or hidden. This is a summary, not legal advice.

Content rights and reuse

The creator usually owns the content they make. If you want to use their photographs on your website, in OTA galleries on MakeMyTrip, Booking.com or Airbnb, in ads or in print, agree that in writing:

  • Which uses are allowed (organic social, website, OTAs, paid ads, print).
  • For how long (for example, one year, or indefinitely).
  • Whether you must credit them, and how.
  • Whether you receive the original files.

Paid ad usage is often priced separately. For how creator content fits into your visual library, see our post on resort photography and video.

Measure enquiries and bookings, not just views

Views and likes tell you a post was seen. They do not tell you whether anyone booked. Set up simple tracking before the post goes live:

  • A unique link to your booking page with UTM tags, so visits show up in Google Analytics under the creator's name.
  • A unique offer code (for example, a welcome drink or late checkout) for direct bookings.
  • A pre-filled WhatsApp message link that mentions the creator, so you can see which enquiries came from their audience.
  • A note in your booking records for any guest who says they found you through the creator.

Review results a few weeks after posting and again at the end of the season. Our analytics and reporting page explains how this tracking is usually set up, and our post on what data to track covers the wider picture.

Frequently asked questions

How do I find the right travel creators for my property?

Start with people already close to you: past guests who post about travel, creators who have tagged your destination, and those followed by your own guests. Search Instagram for your location and nearby places. Then check audience location, the kind of people commenting and how they covered other stays before you reach out.

Is a free stay enough payment for a creator?

For smaller creators and simple deliverables, a complimentary stay is often accepted. For larger creators, longer video or content you plan to reuse in ads, a fee is usually expected. Whatever the arrangement, put the deliverables and rights in writing, and remember the stay itself must be disclosed as a material connection.

What happens if a creator does not disclose the collaboration?

Ask them to add a clear label promptly. ASCI's guidelines expect advertisers to make sure influencer posts are compliant and to ask for non-compliant posts to be edited or removed. Include disclosure in your written brief from the start so there is no confusion about what is expected.

Can I repost a creator's content on my own Instagram?

Sharing their post to your stories with credit is common, but using their photos or video in your own posts, website, OTA listings or ads needs their permission. Agree the uses, duration and credit in writing before the stay, and ask for the original files if you plan to reuse them.

Where to start

List five past guests or local creators whose audience resembles your best guests, and check their audience insights before contacting anyone. Draft a one-page brief with deliverables, disclosure, content rights and a tracking link, and offer the first collaboration on midweek or off-season dates.
